3 Burden of Proof
4 Our analysis of this case begins with the burden of proof.
5 The valuation placed on the property by the assessor is presumed
6 to be correct and can only be overcome by presentation of clear,
7 cogent, and convincing evidence that the value is erroneous. RCW
8 84. 40. 0301. " Clear, cogent, and convincing" evidence means a
9 quantum of proof that is less than beyond a reasonable doubt, but
10 more than a mere preponderance of the evidence. It is the quantum
11 of evidence necessary to convince the trier of fact that the
12 ultimate fact in issue is " highly probable." In re Sego, 82 Wn. 2d
13 736, 513 P. 2d 831 ( 1973).
14
15 True and Fair Value
16 RCW 84. 40. 030( 1) provides criteria for the true and fair
17 value of real property for taxation purposes as follows:
18 Any sales of the property being appraised or
similar properties with respect to sales made in the
19 past five years. The appraisal shall be consistent
with the comprehensive land use plan, development
20 regulations under chapter 36. 70A RCW, zoning, and any
other governmental policies or practices in effect at
21 the time of appraisal that affect the use of property,
as well as physical and environmental influences. An
22 assessment may not be determined by a method that
assumes a land usage not permitted, for that property
23 being appraised, under existing zoning or land use
planning ordinances or statutes. The appraisal shall

effective market demand for property of such type, in
4 the geographical area in which such property is

7 Analyzing sale prices of similar property is the most reli-
8 able method for determining value if adequate data is available.
9 Shahalee Country Club, Inc. v. Board of Tax Appeals, 108 Wn. 2d 26,
10 735 P. 2d 1320 ( 1987); B. Boyce and W. Kinnard, Jr., Appraising
11 Real Property 199 ( 1984). We find there is adequate comparable
12 sales data presented by the Assessor for properties that are
13 sufficiently similar to the subject to support his assessed value
14 determinations.

16 The Assessor is required to establish the true and fair value
17 of property based upon sales of the subject property or sales of
18 comparable properties made within the past five years. True and
19 fair value is " market value," that is, the price to be paid by a
20 willing buyer to a willing seller. Carkonen v. Williams, 76 Wn. 2d
21 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969).

1 Environmental and Land Use Matters
2 The Owners and the Assessor have stipulated to a set of nine
3 environmental and land use restrictions that impact and constrain
4 the Owners' use of the property. The Owners contend the Assessor
5 must take these conditions into consideration when determining
6 fair market value. The Assessor testified this requirement is met
7 through use of comparable property sales within the general area
8 that are subject to similar restrictions and limitations. We find
9 the Assessor has done so.
10
11 The market value of similarly situated property located in
12 the same general area and subject to similar conditions and
13 restrictions is the best indicator of true and fair value. RCW
14 84. 40. 0301( 1). The Owners believe the environmental and land use
15 restrictions limit the use and therefore the value of the prop-
16 erty. These restrictions ought to be reflected in the assessed
17 value, they say. The Assessor counters that prices paid for
18 similarly impacted properties fronting the Raging River indicate
19 willing buyers pay a market price for similar properties with
20 similar restrictions and limitations. We agree with the Assessor.
21
22 The sales comparison approach relies on the economic prin-
23 ciples of supply and demand, substitution, and contribution. The
24 interactions of supply and demand factors determine property

1 prices. One factor that impacts demand is the costof substitute
2 properties. The economic principle of substitution states that a
3 prudent buyer will pay no more for a property than for a compa-

7 Raging River, the prevailing environmental and use restrictions,
8 while limiting the unfettered use of a property, support features

11 similarly situated properties of similar utility.
